lessons.title: Black Monday 1987: The Fastest Fall on Record

body.text: In October 1987 there was no war, no bank collapse and no recession. The market fell 22.6% in a single day mainly because of how investors were selling, not because of what they were selling.

children.text: Black Monday is the largest one day percentage fall in the history of the Dow Jones Industrial Average. It is also one of the most important crashes to study, because it breaks the usual story. There was no single piece of news big enough to explain it. Instead, a popular risk management strategy, run by computers and followed by giant institutions, turned an ordinary sell-off into a free fall. If you trade in a market where algorithms now place a large share of orders, 1987 is not ancient history.
The Setup: A Five Year Bull Run

From its August 1982 low, the Dow rose more than threefold in five years. By 1987 there were real worries in the background: rising interest rates, a weakening US dollar, a large trade deficit, rising oil prices and tensions between the US and Iran. None of these was new, and none looked like a reason for a 20% one day fall. Markets had shrugged them off for months.

children.text: The Machine Inside the Crash: Portfolio Insurance

markDefs.definition: A dynamic hedging strategy popular in the 1980s that protected a portfolio against falls by automatically selling stock index futures as the market declined, and buying them back as it rose.
Contracts to buy or sell a stock index, such as the S&P 500 or the Nifty 50, at a fixed price on a future date. Selling index futures profits when the market falls, so they can hedge a portfolio.

children.text: In the mid 1980s, big US pension funds and institutions adopted a strategy called
portfolio insurance
. The idea sounded sensible: instead of buying costly protection, a computer model would sell
stock index futures

whenever the market fell, and sell more as it fell further. Losses in the shares would be offset by gains on the futures. According to the Brady Commission that later investigated the crash, $60 billion to $90 billion of equities were covered by these strategies by mid October 1987.
The flaw only appears when everyone uses the same strategy at once. Here is the loop it created:
The market falls, so portfolio insurance models tell institutions to sell index futures.
Heavy futures selling pushes futures prices below the value of the underlying shares.
Arbitrage traders buy the cheap futures and sell the actual shares to lock in the gap, pushing share prices down.
The fall in shares triggers the portfolio insurance models to sell even more futures.
Other investors see prices collapsing, cannot find out what is happening fast enough, and sell in panic.

body.title: Portfolio Insurance: The Promise vs The Reality

columns.label: What It Promised
points: Cheaper than buying options for protection
Sell small amounts gradually as the market slips
A buyer would always be there to take the other side

columns.label: What Happened in October 1987
points: Institutions sold into the same falling market at the same time
Selling was forced by models, regardless of price
Markets gapped down, so gradual selling was impossible
Buyers vanished precisely when the models needed them most
The strategy protected no one and deepened the fall for everyone

body.title: Spot the Flaw
body.question: Portfolio insurance works reasonably well for one fund. Why did it fail so badly in October 1987?
options: The computers used to run it crashed on the day
Stock index futures were banned on 19 October
So many institutions followed the same sell-as-it-falls rule that their combined selling became the fall itself
The strategy only worked for individual stocks, not indices
body.explanation: A strategy that relies on selling into a falling market assumes someone else will buy. When tens of billions of dollars of portfolios follow the same rule, the rule creates a wall of automatic selling that feeds on itself. This is the same forced seller problem you met in Lesson 1.3, except the force came from a model rather than a margin call.

children.text: Five Days in October

events.title: The Warning Week
events.description: Markets fall steadily. On Friday 16 October, the Dow drops 108.35 points to about 2,247.06. Portfolio insurance models end the week with a large backlog of futures still to sell.

events.title: Asia and Europe Fall First
events.description: Markets in Asia and Europe open sharply lower. When New York opens, many large stocks cannot begin trading for some time because there are far more sellers than buyers.

events.title: Black Monday
events.description: The Dow falls 508.32 points, or 22.6%, to 1,738.74. It is still the Dow's largest one day percentage fall ever. Price reports run so far behind that investors do not know what their orders will fill at.

events.title: The Fed Steps In
events.description: Before markets open, the Federal Reserve announces it stands ready to provide liquidity to the financial system. Banks keep lending to brokers and traders. After a terrifying morning, markets stabilise.

events.title: Hong Kong Shuts Its Doors
events.description: The Hong Kong Stock Exchange suspends trading for four days to stop the panic. The pressure simply builds up.

events.title: Hong Kong Reopens
events.description: The Hang Seng falls by about a third on reopening. Closing the market delayed the fall but did not prevent it.

events.title: A Surprising Year End
events.description: Despite the crash, the Dow finishes 1987 with a small gain for the year. The S&P 500 regains its pre-crash high by July 1989.

body.label: What the Brady Commission Found About 19 October
body.context: Just three portfolio insurers accounted for nearly $2 billion of the roughly $21 billion of shares sold on the NYSE that day, about 10% of all selling from three institutions following automatic rules. Other institutions following similar reactive strategies added more.

body.title: Your Turn: Measure the Full Damage
body.prompt: The Dow closed at its peak of 2,722.42 on 25 August 1987. On Black Monday it closed at 1,738.74. Using the drawdown method from Lesson 1.1, what was the total fall from peak to the Black Monday close? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Drawdown = (2722.42 minus 1738.74) divided by 2722.42, times 100, which is about 36.1%. Black Monday itself was 22.6%, but the market was already down about 17.5% before that day. Headlines remember the single day. Investors lived through the whole drawdown.

children.text: Why 1987 Did Not Become 1929

markDefs.definition: A central bank's role of lending to banks and the financial system during a crisis, when private lenders pull back, to prevent a panic from causing a collapse. In India, RBI performs this role.

children.text: On paper, 1987 looked just as frightening as 1929. The single day fall was far bigger. The difference was the response. On the morning of 20 October, the Federal Reserve under Alan Greenspan issued a short statement: it "affirmed today its readiness to serve as a source of liquidity" to the economic and financial system. The Fed was acting as the
lender of last resort
, and it pushed banks to keep lending to the brokers and traders who needed cash to settle trades.

cells: Automated portfolio insurance selling by institutions
Allowed the money supply to shrink by about a third
Promised liquidity the next morning and kept credit flowing
Growth continued, and no recession followed immediately
Dow back at its peak in 1954
S&P 500 back at its pre-crash high by July 1989

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: When a central bank promises to lend to the financial system during a panic, it is acting as the lender of last ___.
body.explanation: The lender of last resort idea is the single biggest reason 1987 did not repeat 1929. In India, RBI plays this role, as it did in March 2020 when it cut rates and injected liquidity into the banking system.

children.text: The Legacy: Circuit Breakers in the US and India

markDefs.definition: Automatic, exchange-wide trading halts triggered when a benchmark index moves by a set percentage in a day, designed to interrupt panic and let orders and information catch up.

children.text: One of the Brady Commission's key recommendations was a mechanism to pause trading when markets move too violently, giving investors time to process information and giving the system time to catch up. These
market-wide circuit breakers

were introduced in the US after 1987. India adopted index-based market-wide circuit breakers on 2 July 2001. They trigger at 10%, 15% and 20% moves in either the Sensex or the Nifty 50, whichever is breached first, and halt trading across all equity and equity derivative markets nationwide.

body.text: A circuit breaker is a pause button, not a floor. In March 2020, India's circuit breakers halted trading twice, on 13 and 23 March, yet the Nifty still fell about 38% from its peak. What a halt does is break the feedback loop for a while, so that decisions are made by people rather than by a runaway cycle of automatic orders.

children.text: Could a Machine-Driven Crash Happen in India? For a Few Minutes, It Did

On the morning of 5 October 2012, the Nifty collapsed by more than 15% within moments. There was no economic news. A dealer at the brokerage Emkay Global, executing a basket order for an institutional client, entered the value of the order in the quantity field. The result was 59 erroneous sell orders worth over ₹650 crore, which swept through every buy order in the book. At 9:50:58 am the index circuit filter was triggered and NSE halted the cash market. Trading resumed after the halt, and prices recovered, but the trades that had already executed stood.

body.title: Fat Finger, Algorithm or Portfolio Insurance: What Is the Difference?

children.text: All three can cause sudden, violent moves, but they fail in different ways:
Fat finger error:
a human enters the wrong number, as in the 2012 NSE flash crash. The damage is a one-off burst of bad orders, and prices usually recover quickly once the error stops.
Algorithmic trading gone wrong:
a program keeps placing orders based on flawed logic or unexpected data. It can repeat the mistake thousands of times a second until someone switches it off.
Crowded strategy, as in 1987:

each institution's model works correctly, but so many follow similar rules that their combined behaviour creates a feedback loop. This is the most dangerous kind, because no single error can be fixed.

Exchanges now use pre-trade risk checks, price bands on individual stocks, order value limits and circuit breakers to contain all three. SEBI has also brought in a framework for algorithmic trading by retail investors, requiring algo orders to be tagged and routed through approved brokers.

body.title: The Stop-Loss That Fired at the Worst Price
body.scenario: It is 5 October 2012. You hold shares of a large Nifty company bought at ₹1,000, now trading at ₹1,040. To protect yourself, you placed a stop-loss market order to sell if the price hits ₹950. At 9:50 am the flash crash hits. Your stop-loss triggers, and your market order fills at ₹842 in the chaos. Fifteen minutes later, after the halt, the stock is back at ₹1,035. The exchange confirms the trades will not be cancelled.
body.prompt: What went wrong with your order, and how would you set up protective orders differently to reduce this risk in the future?
body.modelAnswer: The stop-loss worked exactly as designed, which was the problem. A stop-loss market order (SL-M) becomes a market order the moment the trigger price is hit, and a market order accepts whatever price is available. In a flash crash, the buy orders in the book are wiped out, so the next available price can be far below the trigger. You were sold at ₹842, a 15.8% loss from ₹1,000, instead of the 5% loss you planned at ₹950, and the price then recovered. To reduce this risk: first, use a stop-loss limit order (SL) rather than SL-M where possible, setting a limit price below the trigger (for example, a trigger at ₹950 and a limit at ₹930), so the order will not fill below a price you choose. The trade-off is that in a genuine crash, a limit order might not fill at all. Second, avoid placing tight stop-losses on long-term holdings you would be happy to hold through a temporary panic. Third, remember that stop-losses offer no protection against gaps, where a stock opens far below your trigger. Protective orders are tools for managing risk, not guarantees of a price.

body.title: Protect Your Orders From a Fast Market
steps: Open your broker's order window, such as Zerodha Kite, and find the difference between SL (stop-loss limit) and SL-M (stop-loss market) orders
Review every open stop-loss order you have and note whether it is a market or limit type
For each limit stop-loss, check that the gap between trigger and limit price is realistic for that stock's daily volatility
Avoid placing large market orders in the first few minutes after the market opens, when prices move fastest
Look up the daily price band for each stock you hold on NSE, so you know how far it can move in a day
Decide in advance which holdings you would hold through a sudden temporary crash, and remove tight stop-losses on those

cards.definition: 19 October 1987, when the Dow fell 22.6% in a single day, its largest one day percentage fall ever.
A 1980s hedging strategy that automatically sold stock index futures as markets fell. When widely used, it amplified the crash.
Contracts to buy or sell an index at a fixed price on a future date. Selling them gains when the market falls.
The US presidential task force that investigated the 1987 crash and recommended reforms, including circuit breakers.
A central bank lending to the financial system in a crisis when private lenders pull back. RBI plays this role in India.
An exchange-wide trading halt triggered by a set index move. In India, at 10%, 15% and 20% on the Sensex or Nifty 50, since 2001.
An extremely rapid fall and recovery in prices within minutes, often caused by erroneous or automated orders, as on NSE on 5 October 2012.

points: On 19 October 1987 the Dow fell 22.6% in one day, with no single piece of news big enough to explain it
Portfolio insurance, used on $60 billion to $90 billion of equities, created a feedback loop of automatic futures selling and arbitrage selling of shares
Strategies that are safe for one investor can become dangerous when everyone follows the same rule at the same time
The Fed's promise of liquidity on 20 October, acting as lender of last resort, is the main reason 1987 did not become another 1929
Circuit breakers came out of the 1987 crash, and India introduced index-based market-wide circuit breakers at 10%, 15% and 20% on 2 July 2001
NSE's 2012 flash crash showed that fast markets can fill stop-loss market orders at extreme prices, so understand the difference between SL and SL-M orders
